Adult specimens of Elongate ilisha (Ilisha elongata) commonly attain a maximum standard length of 49.8 cm [Li = 49.8 cm], corresponding to a total length of roughly 60 cm, making it one of the larger members of the Pristigasteridae family. Field surveys conducted in the coastal waters of the western Pacific indicate that this species experiences relatively rapid early growth, with individuals reaching puberty at a standard length of approximately 22 cm [Lp = approximately 22 cm]. This size at maturation suggests a moderately early onset of reproductive capability, particularly when compared to other clupeiform fishes that delay reproduction until a larger proportion of their asymptotic size is achieved. The ultimate wet weight of adults has been estimated at 1.6 kg [Wwi = 1.6 kg], a value derived from length-weight regressions fitted to a large sample of commercially harvested fish. Such a body mass places this species at the upper end of the size spectrum within its genus, with implications for its energetic demands and trophic position as a mid-level planktivore.

At the onset of reproductive life, individuals of Ilisha elongata typically achieve a wet weight at puberty of approximately 139 grams [Wwp = approximately 139 grams], reflecting the substantial somatic investment required before the first spawning event can occur. This value, estimated from the same length-weight relationship, represents a threshold below which gonadal development is unlikely to be initiated. The ovaries of gravid females contain numerous small, pelagic eggs with a mean diameter of about 2 mm, and the estimated dry weight of each fertilized ovum is 0.0042 grams [Wwb = 0.0042 grams], a mass typical of species that produce yolk-rich, pelagic propagules. Following fertilization, the eggs undergo rapid cleavage and embryogenesis, a process that is highly temperature-dependent. Under experimental incubation conditions maintained at 27.9 °C [T = 27.9 °C], the time from fertilization to eclosion is approximately 6 days [ab = approximately 6 days], a duration that aligns well with published data for other warm-water clupeiforms such as Engraulis encrasicolus.

The yolk-sac larvae that emerge after the 6-day incubation period (6 days) [ab = 6 days] are lecithotrophic, relying entirely on endogenous yolk reserves for the first several days post-hatch at a temperature of 27.9 °C [T = 27.9 °C]. These prolarvae, measuring only a few millimeters in length, possess a transparent, non-pigmented body and a prominent yolk sac that is gradually resorbed as the mouth opens and the retina differentiates. The transition to exogenous feeding, marked by first prey capture and the onset of active foraging in the plankton, represents a critical bottleneck in early life history. Under the same thermal regime of 27.9 °C [T = 27.9 °C], the yolk-sac resorption period is brief, and larvae must encounter suitable zooplankton densities within a narrow temporal window to avoid starvation. The maximum lifespan of this species, based on otolith-based age estimates from wild-caught specimens, is approximately 10 years [am = approximately 10 years] when evaluated at the ambient temperature of 27.9 °C [T = 27.9 °C], a longevity that is consistent with an iteroparous, multiple-spawning life history.

Life-history theory predicts that a species with an age at birth of only 6 days [ab = 6 days] will exhibit a relatively fast pace of life, characterized by early maturation and high reproductive output, a pattern broadly confirmed for Ilisha elongata at a temperature of 27.9 °C [T = 27.9 °C]. The maximum lifespan of 10 years [am = 10 years] recorded in fish maintained at 27.9 °C [T = 27.9 °C] is moderate compared to long-lived clupeids such as those in the genus Alosa, but the iteroparous strategy of Ilisha elongata allows for multiple reproductive seasons spanning several years, given that puberty is attained at a standard length of just 22 cm [Lp = 22 cm]. Gravid individuals sampled from spawning aggregations in the South China Sea display a standard length approaching 49.8 cm [Li = 49.8 cm], confirming that the species can continue somatic growth well after the onset of reproduction. The wet weight of such reproductively active adults, reaching as much as 1.6 kg [Wwi = 1.6 kg], underscores the substantial body size that supports the production of large batches of pelagic eggs.

Recruitment success in Ilisha elongata is tightly linked to oceanic conditions, as the pelagic larvae are highly susceptible to advection away from favorable nursery grounds. The estimated dry weight at birth of 0.0042 grams [Wwb = 0.0042 grams] per egg reflects a maternal investment strategy that prioritizes fecundity over per-offspring provisioning, a common adaptation in marine teleosts that broadcast numerous small eggs. The wet weight of 139 grams [Wwp = 139 grams] at first reproduction indicates that females must accumulate considerable lipid reserves before vitellogenesis, a process that may take several months of intensive feeding during the pre-spawning season. Comparative analysis with the congener Ilisha megaloptera reveals that Ilisha elongata reaches a larger ultimate size, as its maximum standard length of 49.8 cm [Li = 49.8 cm] exceeds that of its smaller relative by roughly 10 cm. Field observations of schooling behavior suggest that this species undertakes seasonal inshore migrations for spawning, likely timed to coincide with periods of elevated primary productivity that ensure adequate food for the rapidly developing larvae.
